Zaha Hadid. The Iraqi-British architect pioneering parametric and computational design to create sweeping, flowing forms that defied Euclidean geometry and established her as a leading visionary of twenty-first-century architecture.

Hadid lived from 1950 until her unexpected death in 2016. She designed the MAXXI, the National Museum of Twenty-First Century Arts in Rome, completed in 2010. It's a fluid concrete structure with soaring interior galleries that seems to defy traditional museum constraints. She created the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan in 2012, a smooth, billowing white building with no sharp corners that epitomizes her flowing, organic computational aesthetic.

Hadid pioneered parametric design, using mathematical algorithms and computational modeling to generate complex, efficient forms impossible to design by hand. She designed the London Aquatics Centre for the 2011 Olympics, a steel and membrane structure evoking the fluidity of water while meeting Olympic competition standards.

She studied under Rem Koolhaas at the Architectural Association, absorbing deconstructivist principles before innovating her own flowing language. Her work rejected the box-like International Style, instead creating buildings that appeared to move and shift, celebrating curves and motion. In 2004, she won the Pritzker Prize, becoming the first woman to win architecture's highest honor, though many of her landmark works were completed after this recognition.

Her contemporary Frank Gehry also explored curved, deconstructed forms through digital design, and both pushed modernism toward sculptural expressionism. Her work advanced the philosophical movement of deconstruction through computational means. She was influenced by her mentor Rem Koolhaas, and both rejected conventional architectural logic in their designs.
